Once together the unit feels stable, sturdy and fairly safe (though all of these small fire bowls are hazardous if used improperly), and looks good, too.You aren't going to be putting large logs in this fire pit, and the included cover is extremely flimsy (ripped on our second use), but this is an otherwise good-looking, solid fire bowl, perfect for roasting marshmallows or just backyard ambiance. The beautiful cooper bowl did immediately discolor with use, but that's to be expected, though it does kind of diminish its appeal.I like that there is also a screen to put over the top to protect little ones, and lawns and homes, from sparks. Once it's on though you can't remove it, for instance, for additional marshmallow roasting, because the metal handle will quickly get untouchably hot (duh!), so only put it on AFTER you're done using the open flame. (And even then we used fire tongs to do so.) You could, kind of, roast on the heat coming through the grate, but we lost two marshmallows on it that way and it was pretty messy (melted marshmallow remains today), so I wouldn't recommend.Of course, be sure you're using the pit on a stable, fireproof surface (concrete or stone recommended) as putting this on your lawn is just asking for trouble ... In the form of a tipping bowl of fire onto a flammable surface. Not a good plan. Also, make sure all fires are fully extinguished and be aware that fire bowls are usually NOT exempt from burn bans, so please check and make sure they're allowed and safe in your are before using this or any other outdoor fireplace item. In short: be smart, be safe and if in doubt, don't set anything, including yourself, on fire, OK? :)Currently, it's pretty pricey for what you get, and the bowl discoloration and worthless cover almost made me rate this three stars, rather than four, but in the end we enjoyed it enough and it felt well-built so I went with four, but it was a close call.
summary: Easy to Assemble, Feels Sturdy But Some Weaknesses

reviewText: This fire pit comes with all you see in the picture, plus a tool so you can lift the lid once the fire is lit a vinyl cover to protect it.  So assembly is easy, if you do it the right way the first time, lol.  My husband is great at assembly required projects and has even built many wonderful things from scratch.  My husband looked at the pieces and said "this doesn't make sense" they way they have the bolt, screw, and washer connect to the bowl so he put it together the way he thought it should be, and it was wobbly.  Then, he figured out the legs have to be on a certain side for the base to fit so that it has a stable base.  So, he took it apart and put it back together, and it holds together fine.  Unlike other reviewers, it hasn't moved on its own or made noise, despite recent bad weather so ours seems stable.  I agree with one reviewer being puzzled by the suggestion of sand at the bottom of the bowl, when it has holes in the bowl.  We put tiny stones.  Perhaps they don't want you to put a fire directly in the fire pit, but that seems to me to defeat the purpose for some people to have to buy extra things for it to be safe. We already had the tiny stones. When I read about not putting it on the deck and then what they said about sand, it made me wonder if they said those things so people can't sue them, lol.  We got it for free because I review for Amazon vine, so can't speak whether it is worth the cost, but those that paid for it seem to think not.  It looks great, but of course you want to be able to use a fire pit safely.  I will send updates if anything happens to the product after we have used it more times.So to recap for us it is stable, looks great, and is usable.
summary: Works fine for us in the end

reviewText: This was easy to assemble and it looks like a great product. It is assembled by screwing in a three inch bolt that holds the legs together to form a base. The top ring on the wire mesh simple screws into the metal at the top. I had the whole thing unpacked and assembled in ten minutes. It has several holes in the bottom basin and the instructions say to add several inches of sand. But obviously the sand would run out. Instead it seem like it would be best if you added gravel about the size of your fingernail. I have no idea why the manufacturer suggested adding sand. It has been too cold to barbecue here so I will give an update how it works with a fire as soon as the weather warms up.

The bowl is 28" in diameter and 27.5" high. This is big enough for a small/medium wood fire, and the bowl is made for use with charcoal, wood, and self-starting fire logs. When the fire pit is assembled, the bowl rim is at about knee-height.I used to own a heavy but movable rectangular metal fire pit. You accessed it by side doors that were tilted to form a V top and didn't open widely (though they could be removed). That design made it awkward to put more wood on the fire or to reach in to cook potatoes or such. But the open design of this fire bowl makes it very easy to use.The mesh wire dome spark guard was fine enough to keep ash in, high enough not to warp from heat unless you make a big fire, and easy to remove with the provided removal tool which can probably double as a poker. The dome spark guard sits in a 1" depression on the inside edge of the fire bowl rim so that a strong gust of wind or small dog can't easily knock the cover off.The bowl also came with a small, circle, black-coated grill. It sits about 1.5" off the bowl's bottom at the deepest point. This seems pretty low to me, especially if you put the 1" of sand on the bottom, as recommended, for even heat distribution. But I don't use grills. My brother, who does, said he liked that low height because once the coals are at a good cooking heat then you don't want the food too far away from them.The fire bowl also came with a vinyl cover that you can put over your (not-hot) spark guard and fire bowl to protect them from the weather. This cover wasn't a struggle to put on yet still fit snugly over the rim of the fire bowl. The fire bowl/pit is also easy enough to move and assemble that you can take it down or move it out of the weather to protect it from rusting.For those who haven't used something like this before: hot fires will warp the metal screen, use will discolor the metal inside the bowl, and the paint will eventually wear off. The directions do tell you how to clean and shine the bowl up and re-paint the screen if looks are important to you. These movable fire pits are also meant to be used over non-burnable surfaces, so on concrete or gravel or dirt. They aren't meant to be used on a wooden porch or inside.When I first opened the fire pit package, my impression was of a beautiful design and solid materials that would last. Everything you need to assemble the fire bowl (including the tools) were included. The only real assembly was to screw the handle into the fireguard and to screw the two base legs together to form an X. The base held together pretty well even without the screw and was not wobbly until the screw was tightened. I left the screw as snug but not extremely tight and the wobble was minimal on a flat surface and unnoticeable on an uneven surface. You place the bowl on the base. The bowl's outside rim edge curves down to form a ridge that holds the bowl in place. The bowl might shift slightly if bumped or the whole assembly might skid sideways, but it's unlikely the bowl will come off the base unless lifted. The bowl is light enough that a woman or teenager can easily lift and move it for storage or removing ash.The fire bowl's bottom is several inches above the X of the base's legs. According to the directions, the bowl is not secured to the legs (nor does there appear any need for this). There are also 5 holes along the bottom of the bowl to allow better air flow. Very little ash falls through these holes even if you're stirring the fire or removing the ash. Even a soft breeze creates an air flow through the bowl that keeps the fire burning hot and fast which creates a pile of hot coals. These coals keep burning hot for several hours. I've found the bowl good for quickly burning up small wood (2" or less diameter wood) and for cooking. I haven't tried thicker wood yet.Overall, it looks like a lot of thought went into this design to make it usable and beautiful.
summary: Beautiful look, easy to assemble and use

reviewText: I really liked the look of this fire pit and thought it would be a great addition to the backyard.  However, as we were setting it up, we knocked it over at least four times.  I think it's just a little too high off the ground for my taste.  I refer a fire pit that rides the ground a bit more in case of sparks or, like us, people running into it or knocking it over.  It does have a nice, deep bowl, and the screen is very nice if you're in an area that doesn't allow open fires.  All in all, a nice fire it if you have it in an area that's away from someone tripping on it or knocking it over.

All excitement about this fire pit went out the window as soon as I placed the base of the fire pit on the ground. As many other reviewers have mentioned, this fire pit is extremely wobbly and does not rest flush against the ground, which drove me absolutely crazy as I tried figuring out whether or not my brick patio was uneven. I even went and grabbed a level to make sure of it, and after getting positive confirmation, I knew with certainty that this fire pit is uneven, which is an absolute shame because the pictures make it look extremely stylish. As for the other parts, you can tell they are of relatively low quality, and nothing at all really seems to fit just right on this fire pit. There are better options out there, especially considering the price, so take a pass on this poorly made offering.
summary: Great Design Trumped By Poor Quality

reviewText: This is over $200 and I'd say it's worth, maybe $49 to $79. Even then, I'd look for a better product in any price range. It was easy enough to put together, even for me, but when I put it on it's feet it was so not substantial. It reminds me of these super cheap bar stools we got once...no one ever sat in them because they just felt cheap and wobbly.When I read that I could not use this on my deck, I was even more disappointed. You have to drag it out into the yard to use it, where I already have a nice, sturdy, rock fire pit. In the grass it was a little less tippy, but all-in-all I'd pass on this one. I had one fire in it and kept the hose very close-by in case it just crashed to the ground. I am going to let it air out a bit and use it on my deck, filling it with flowers.
summary: Yeesh, this thing is so flimsy!

reviewText: When looking at this product I see something sleek and modern with appealing aesthetics, but beyond that there is nothing I can find that would make this product worth getting. When making the decision on a fire pit quality of the materials used should be a deciding factor, this could make a big difference in how long the pit lasts. There were quite a few pieces for assembly and once they were all together the pit was unstable and rocked back and forth like the legs were uneven, something that can not possibly be safe, and the bowl is thin which also seems unsafe. The only way I can see this thing lasting longer than a few months is for someone to build a paver wall around it (for stability) and to NEVER move it because this stand/base seems like it wouldn't last more than a few moves around the patio.
summary: Lacking the quality to be a good product.

reviewText: Well, I'm setting here wondering what positive to say on this item. Its poorly built, flimsy and  reeks of the words "fire hazard." The way it is put together is easy enough, unfortunately in all the wrong ways. That's terribly disappointing, too, because I had high hopes for this item, imagining myself enjoying it while taking to the summer - when it finally comes. The cost, to me at least, seems astounding, considering how flimsy the build on it is. Really, the wind moves it around outside, causing it to shift back and forth every few minutes.It looks cool anyhow; and considering that's all I can do with it and feel safe, I guess that's a mild something.

I have put this trap outside, where the disgusting critters tend to hang out now that summer is approaching.  I prefer it outside, so that Freak, my trusty mouse catcher,  will not bring them inside.... if they are killed outside first.This is easy to set.  I will update on a catch.  The trap has three entrances, great for multiple catches.  Any mouse catcher that does not have visible catches, is a great thing.  I hate to see mice on a trap....gross.So, once you catch mice, you can dispose of it, or reset it.  This is much safer to use than those old fashioned traps.  Place it along the wall if necessary, the trap has a spring loaded choker that will kill mice quickly.  .....Rizzo

Having used the Victor Flea traps with great success (well, no I am not inundated with them but a recent flea-to-cat infestation in one room only, made me bring out the big guns, including Victor flea traps), I decided to try the Victor Tri Kill Mouse trap, since I have had (unwanted) mice in this apartment in the past.I set up the Victor Tri-Kill Mouse Trap in front of my kitchen sink cabinet -- this is a place where mice have been known to frequent, and although I closed up all their  entraceways, as well as the holes under the sink, I'm sure there are a few persistent mice and I can only hope this tri-trap catches them. My cats are not allowed in the kitchen, so there's no chance that they will find and play with these traps (although they have been very talented at finding and playing with mice in the past).I did not have peanut butter -- I hope high-end cashew butter works just as well. It took me a while to stop all the flipping and clicking of the doors -- I was finally able to set this down in its appointed place, and ... well, we shall see what happens. I am not squeamish -- I have never been known to squeam at anything. My experiences with mice usually entails my putting on a rubber glove and grabbing the little stinkers dead or alive, sometimes literally out of the mouths of one or the other of my quite-miffed cats. (Management puts out posion baits for these mice downstairs -- I don't want my cats to eat a poisoned mouse)And if I can't get to the trap in time to remove whatever dead body (bodies) happen to be languishing in it, I can only wonder what the other mice will do when they see one of their own sticking out of it, hopelessly strangled. Time will tell. Thank you Victor.UPDATE -- No victims yet --  nothing more than a few clicks and clacks when these traps have opened up unexpectedly. I think the plastic retainer-tab is a little too weak to do a proper job.UPDATE May 2013 -- Clicking and Clacking -- the spring loaded tabs will not remain in their set positions. Time to go back and design a better Mouse trap.
summary: Not too happy with this design

reviewText: This product is designed to capture tiny mice. Mice around where i am are not giant, but not tiny mice. I guess your average mouse is not tiny. It can catch an average sized mouse, but the noise and movement of the mouse inside stops any other mouse from being caught. And it is not big enough to catch large mice (not rats which is definitely not possible)

First I must state that my 'for review' Tri-Kill hasn't killed or caught any mice yet. Our mouse-invasion season is usually October-November when field mice seek warmth and shelter in our basement which is a bad idea because they all end up caught.With that in mind, we developed a pretty good understanding of what works and what doesn't when it comes to mouse defense. The ultrasound deterrents, for example do not seem to work. Mouse traps do but mice are smart and it's unlikely you'll catch more than one mouse with the same trap placed at the same location and one trap rarely catches more than 2 or 3 even if you move it around the basement. What works with mice is 'variety' and a bait that's hard to resist and hard to get to, unless the mouse enters the trap. The Tri-Kill therefore adds to the 'variety' arsenal, which is a good thing and there's no way the mouse get get close to the bait - peanut butter - unless the mouse enters the trap, another plus. Now, will the Tri-Kill ever catch more than once mouse at a time? I am highly skeptical of that because, like I said, mice are smart and they learn fast so I can't imagine how mouse number 2 would ever try to get to the bait while mouse number 1 is dead or struggling but I will be happy to come back and update this review once I see 2 or 3 mice caught in the Tri-Kill.Finally, the makers claim that this is a no-touch design. Now, I don't know what the definition of 'no-touch' is but the trap has no floor so, whatever the mice do while dying (use imagination) is going to be left on the floor. It would be difficult to avoid touching the kill while disposing of it unless you wear gloves but then all traps could be called 'no touch'.Three stars, by the way, stand for 'It's OK'. I will improve my rating once I see actual mice being caught.

We got all excited at our home when we discovered the first mouse of the season. When I say excited, I don't mean in a good way. >:-<. Not happy at all.First we gave a long lecture to the cats about their proper responsibilities. They seemed suitably impressed as they licked their paws and gave us the "bored cat" look. Somehow, I didn't count on their assistance!So we now have three chihuahuas, two cats, and a six year old to worry about in setting the traps. How to catch one little mouse without endangering any of them.I first tried the little one that uses the rubber band that snaps off onto the mouse. OOOPS, within a couple of minutes our rescue chihuahua had found it and been "shot" by the rubber band. She has probably sworn off peanut butter for life.Since I had just received this from Vine, I thought I'd give it a try. It seemed suitably pet safe.So we put the peanut butter on the bottom and set the trap. First we dealt with the six yer old who wanted to know if the mouse would eat the peanut butter after we caught it. (We said yes).  Five minutes later I walk in and discover the youngest of the dogs with the trap carefully turned over, licking the peanut butter off of the bottom. Sigh.We waited till the dogs were in their kennels for the night and reset it. Sadly, the trap worked about as well as the cats - nothing caught so far.I suspect time will tell, and am continuing to use this. Last year, my husband set multiple traps and injured multiple fingers. We joked about our husband "catch and release" program. This trap is very easy to set and can catch up to three mice at a time. It really works pretty much the same as the traditional ones, except the mice need to be tempted inside to be trapped.If this doesn't work, I will go back to the traditional traps and buy a case of band aids. However, if we actually catch mice using this, I will increase the stars to 5 AND buy a bunch more to hide in places the dogs don't go.
summary: Safe around pets - not safe FROM pets

reviewText: The Victor Tri Kill Mouse Trap is easy to bait, easy to set and stays set until triggered by a mouse (no false triggers).  It works as it should.  It also represents no hazard to pets since there is no external snapping part which could injure them. The plastic killing bar is internal.However, the unit is expensive and for many applications, the three mouse capacity will be of questionable utility. In short, most people would empty the trap once triggered by the first mouse.A better and more practical option for many without pets might be the Snap-E Mouse TrapSnap-E Mouse Trap 6 Traps 675253.  Those traps are less expensive, as easy to set, and are quite powerful. You can put out three in different areas for the price of one Victor Tri Kill trap.
summary: Easy to Set, Pet-Safe, But Expensive; Better Option Might Be The Snap-E Mouse Trap

reviewText: Over this winter I've been getting small field mice in my garage looking for a warm place to stay. I've been placing several plastic classic-type (trigger snaps a lid closed on mouse) traps that have worked very well. When I was offered this I was excited to try one that could collect multiple mice. I am very disappointed.It's unclear how this even works to trap the mice (I guess I'll find out if it ever works) as it sits on the floor and the underneath is hollow. I placed this in the same space as the plastic traps and the plastic traps are still collecting mice and this one sits unused.I'll update this if I ever catch a mouse with this. Until then I'll stick with the classic snap closed type of traps.UPDATE: after nearly a week in the garden shed where I know mice are active at times I still haven't caught anything.

I live in a rural setting where mice are par for the course.  Over time I've built up an impressive collection of mouse traps, ranging from those that trap them live to those that kill quickly and humanely.  None of the spring-loaded cheapie traps.  I have other Victor traps and think their quality is generally pretty good.When this arrived I pulled it out of the package and immediately activated one of the flaps.  Figuring out how to reset it was a snap [no pun intended].  I was a little confused where to put the bait but the instructions and diagram are good and I realized my confusion was in thinking I needed a lot more bait than they think I do.  There is a little circle on the underside, marked "bait" and they suggest just a small dab of peanut butter since the mouse should never get to actually remove any of it.The idea behind this is that the mouse sticks its head through a little rectangle to get to the bait, it releases the spring, and the mouse is choked.  There are 3 openings so technically it can kill 3 before needing to be reset.  (In reality I don't expect to ever actually kill 3 at once since a mouse happening upon a device out of which protrudes 1 or 2 of its dead relatives, is less likely to think it is a good idea to try to get to the bait itself.  Yes, they ARE that smart.)The flaps are very touchy and I set them off multiple times just handling and baiting the trap.  The nice thing though is that there is no danger of personal injury.  The flap springs up - I push it back down.  End of story.The trap is now set and awaiting its first victim.  It has yet to catch anything but I don't count that against the trap because none of my others have caught anything for weeks either.  I know they'll be back but right now I do seem to be enjoying a lull in their activity and that is just fine with me.

Having a house in the suburbs, we get our share of field mice coming to visit.  In the past I have used old-style wood/mental traps.  I later moved on to plastic "jaw" traps which could be staged with food.  I have also used some "hotel" types, where the mouse enters and cannot leave.  I found the second type, the plastic jaw, traps the most effective.  The brand I use is TomCat.  While both these and the wooden style can be reset and reused over and over, I found I had to lay a lot of traps.  To remove a nest of mice, I had to lay several traps, near each other, often perpendicular to one another, to effectively catch and kill the whole nest (which could be 5, 10 or even 20 mice.Victor has been building mousetraps for decades. What I really like about their "Tri Kill" product is that it addresses the need to lay some perpendicular traps.  The layout gives you three traps in one, two at opposing ends of a line, and a third trap perpendicular to the first two, in the middle of them.It also allows you to use less bait (I typically go with peanut butter) since you are putting bait in one, not three, traps.  But since it has three opening and trap points, it can still catch three mice, just like 3 traps.The layout is also nice, as it forces the mouse to enter a hole to investigate/look for bait.  On wooden and plastic jaw traps, I have had some where the mice manage to lick the peanut butter clean, without triggering the trap.Setting it up is simple.  Instructions are on the back of the package. When you take the trap out of the package, you remove the plastic cover from the bottom, bait it (again peanut butter works well) by putting a dab of bait in the circle marked "Bait", and set it somewhere near a wall, or where you've seen activity (mice, droppings, chewing on things).Unlike some other traps where you could catch your finger in it, it is not really possible to hurt yourself with this trap.  You can't really hurt yourself, even if you accidentally trigger it with your finger.Inside each entry is a plastic frame, sort of like a window pane with no glass.  When the mouse sticks his head through the frame, and moves forward, he trips a spring loaded mechanism.  This pulls the frame up and chokes him to the point of suffocation.  It does not, as far as I can see, cause instantaneous death by breaking his neck.  So, it will be fairly quick but not instantaneous.  Sorry to be graphic but "humanely kills" is a usually an oxymoron to me.I recently had some mouse activity in my crawlspace.  I set several of my plastic jaw traps as well as one Tri Kill.  Over the course of a week, both caught mice.  I did have one instance of mice licking the peanut butter clean without setting off the TomCat.  I had another where the TomCat triggered but was unoccupied, so I don't know if it went off by itself, or if a mouse cheated death and narrowly missed being caught.  Without observing in person, it is not possible to tell if a mouse somehow entered the Tri Kill but it failed.  It did catch mice though, and no bait disappeared, so I assume it worked flawlessly.  It was easy enough to empty, dropping the mice into a plastic bag, rinsing and resetting.I would say, all in all, it is just as effective as a conventional trap, perhaps a bit better as the mouse can't easily eat the bait and not get caught.  Also it catches the mouse in pretty much the same position every time, whereas I have conventional traps where sometimes I had a mouse caught by the leg, etc. and you could see it tried to gnaw itself free.You can reuse these or dispose of them.  They do not cause any mess as you are not causing bleeding, etc.  If you do dispose of them with the intent of replacing them each day or in a short time period, it could get expensive, as they sell for $10 or so each.

I'm thinking this is a good product but so far haven't caught any mice. But it is easy to set up and looks like it might do the trick. I do like the fact that you can catch three mice at once. That's a cool addition to the old technology. I'm taking off a star because I don't know if it will catch mice yet. I will update when I catch a mouse.Update: I set the trap last night with a bit of peanut butter as bait (as recommended) and caught two mice. I disposed of them easily and without mess. I easilsy reset the traps without having to replace bait. This is an excellent trap that is easy to use.

I think this is an awesome design and in theory would work well.  The reality is after the first mouse was killed, no more were.  I set this up in an area prone to mice.  What was the problem?  The decomposing smell turned off other mice.  No small amount of peanut butter will overcome rotting mouse stench.
summary: Great design but one major flaw

reviewText: No mice caught so far, but this seems to be a well-designed mousetrap.  The openings are quite small, so I'm not sure if that will be a problem or not.This design seems as if it would be easier to clean up than the more violent designs, although I suppose choking to death isn't exactly a picnic.I'll update this review if or when we catch some mice.  4 stars for now based on price and design.

I like that this mouse trap is preset and ready to go. All you have to do is remove the plastic packaging insert and apply bait (a dab of peanut butter) to the bottom of the trap. This trap is reusable but I found resetting it a bit unreliable. You are supposed to just press down on the tabs but they did not stay in place, and after they finally stayed put, one of the other ones would pop back out. I found it frustrating. In any case, since I don't like dealing with dead mice, I just decided to throw it out after it caught a mouse. So, while this seems like a good trap, it is too expensive to use as a disposable, one time use, trap. It's only reusable if you are willing to physically remove the dead mice.
summary: effective, but there are better alternatives

reviewText: I first liked the way this is shaped like the rat traps I see everywhere.  Rodents like to scurry along walls and dodge into little things, especially if they smell food there.  This is designed to choke them, a more humane method I think than the sticky pads.I like that it can be reused and can be very productive in the first night used.  It's a cool mouse trap.

It took a while but finally it killed two mice. This trap is safer to use than the classic wood traps, so I can leave it just about anywhere I need it.We set it on the garage level. For a month nothing happened. I thought maybe we don't have any more mice, having caught half a dozen earlier this winter. Also, I had bought a bunch of mouse-resistant containers for everything from rice to grass seed so there wasn't much in the house to attract mice except for shelter from cold and wet weather. Well, after a snow storm I spotted a small mouse and then found a second one, caught live in a "humane" plastic box trap. My husband released that one well away from the house and we set out a fresh trap and redid the bait in this Tri-kill trap. Within 24 hours this trap caught and killed two mice! So I guess they came in for shelter from the snow and went for the bait.

The Victor Tri-Kill mousetrap is a nice trap.Pros:It's reusable so it saves money.It can trap 3 mice at a time which is convenient and saves money since you don't have to buy multiple traps.It's safe to use because it doesn't use chemicals or poisons.You don't have to worry about hurting your fingers or getting snapped like a regular traditional mousetrap.Set-up is easy, just take out of the package and bait with peanut butter.Cons:I haven't had any negatives with this mousetrap but the mice don't like it.
summary: Easy to Use and Safe for Hands

reviewText: This trap is very easy to bait and set. I like not using poison because we have pets. We live in the country and mice always come inside when the weather gets cold. Yes we kill them but it is as humane as I care to be. They are attacking us...if they stayed out then I wouldn't bother them. They cause fires and water leaks and all sorts of problems. This trap could just save your house or your life.
I've used this before and even though there was already one dead mouse in the trap it did catch another and it did kill very quickly.I haven't ever caught three at once in it though. Easy to set....

UPDATE: It caught a mouse! Had to have been a clean kill. I disposed of it outside easily without having to touch the mouse. I'm upping the stars by one because the design does actually work. You just have to be careful when setting it not to breathe on it...I really like the design of this trap in theory, the way you can place it against the wall, the fact that you can wash it and reuse it, and also that it won't "bite" human fingers if they are stuck in the trap. However, I had immediate problems with the trap. Once set, it seems to spring open all by itself. After the first night, I found one of the traps sprung open but the trap itself had not moved. I thought "Oh! Crafty mouse!" But then, when I tried to reset it, it kept popping open and the three trap "lids" wouldn't stay closed. I finally got it set, and then while I was standing there looking at it from above, one of the traps popped open again. Am I doing something wrong here?I know we have mice because I see the droppings, but I've never seen them in action. I don't know what size they are, but I expect they are field mice because I've seen a dead one outside. Tiny mice, so they ought to be killed by this trap. But note that the instructions say, "For only a couple of mice, a dozen traps are not too many." Are you kidding me? At ten bucks a trap, I think I'd rather just live with the mice or poison them and put up with the smell of them dying in the walls. Even if they are considering one trap as three, that's still a lot of money compared to the cheaper alternatives.

A cliché in America is that if you build a better mousetrap the world will beat a path to your door. That is what happened to the Victor company which has come out with a modern mousetrap which is the only kind in the world that is capable of killing multiple mice at one time.The Victor Tri-Kill Mouse Trap was engineered with three entrances so it can trap and kill three mice without having to reset the settings. To use, simply apply the bait, place the trap where you want it, and set it. That's it.To bait, you simply turn the trap upside down, add the bait to the area marked "bait here," Then simply place the flat side against a wall for a snug fit and walk away. The traps are set when  you turn it right side up. When the mouse is trapped you can throw the trap away or rebait and reset.This trap is safe to use  when children are around and has a powerful bar for quick and humane killing. Once you try the Victor Tri-Kill you will never return again to using the traditional traps.
summary: This Mouse Trap's 3x As Good As Any Other

reviewText: Goes to show older is better. Based on 1950's design and it worked quickly to catch all our mice.  It will catch yours or your money back, what more can you ask.  "Satisfaction GuaranteedAs the recognized brand leader in rodent control, Victor is committed to making customer satisfaction our number one priority. All of Victor's snap and value added traps are covered under a 30 day warranty."
summary: EASY TO USE, SET AND CLEAN.  A mouse trap that works.

reviewText: This is a 3-holer plastic reuseable mousetrap. The design of the trap is quite different from others on the market. Instead of snapping a bar down on the mouse's spine, this one is designed to jerk the mouse up from below, sort of like a noose. The trap itself is a bit like a roach hotel, with 3 entrances. You put bait in the center of the trap, and when a mouse enters, it must step through a plastic harness before it pushes a door to access the bait. As soon as it pushes that door, the harness jerks up, breaking the mouse's spine. It takes a bit of mass to accomplish this successfully, necessitating a large trap, which is my guess why the trap has 3 holes in one device instead of just 1. The manufacturer notes that mice are social, so where there's one mouse, there's bound to be more--that's probably true, too.I live in an old farm house, so I have plenty of opportunities to test mouse traps, unfortunately. I found this new Tri-Kill trap reasonably easy to bait and set. I put peanut butter as directed in the center of the roof of the trap. To be sure, I also put a small pile of sunflower seeds on the floor and centered the trap over them. And too be extra sure, I made an array of traps, lining up this one, a grey plastic "The Better Mouse Trap" by Intruder, and a black plastic "EZ Set" by Safeguard by the grain bins in my pantry. And which one do the mice prefer? "The Better Mouse Trap" by Intruder, by far. So far, I haven't caught any mice in this Tri-Kill trap. Perhaps the bait, since it is hidden by a swinging door, just isn't prominent enough, at least when other bait is sitting in plain sight on the platter of other traps. "The Better Mouse Trap" is also easy to set, easy to empty, and mice seem to like it a lot (at least once, anyway). I'll keep this Tri-Kill in my arsenal, but "The Better Mouse Trap" is the one that I'll continue to rely on. And yes, while it is good to have more than one trap set if you have a flock of mice, it seems to me, you'd be better off with 3 separate traps than 1 central one with 3 holes, since you can put the 3 separate traps in various places around the room, while this 3 holer locks up all your trap resources into one place.
summary: A New Way to Build a Mousetrap

reviewText: We have a small mouse problem - once or twice a year, a mouse finds its way into our house, and the next day eats the d-Con pellets we put out...then we don't see or hear anything for several months.  (And sometimes a day or two later, we find a small dead mouse.)  This last happened about a month ago.Fast forward to now - this little trap is setup right next to the d-Con bait.  I'll have to update the review later for the status of the kill count, but so far, this mouse trap seems good.  It's easy to setup (rub some peanut butter on a tiny flap of plastic, and push some plastic tabs downward to engage.)  Theory has it that when the mouse goes to eat the PB, it'll trigger the spring and cut the entire mouse in half, with the blood of up to three (blind or not) mice reddening your floors!  I may have made that last part up, and it may just snap the mouse's little neck...but I can't be too sure, as I have not yet had a kill using this mouse trap (and due to Vine review requirements, I can't wait until the First Kill happens.)Overall, it looks like this gadget will work, it set well, and it's actively waiting to kill a mouse.  It is weird that they think somebody will actually want to remove dead mice and reuse the sucker...I'm not THAT environmentally friendly, and you shouldn't be either.  Gross.
summary: Very easy setup...let's hope it works.

reviewText: Victor tri-kill mousetrap does the job ! I got it because we live in the country near a farmers field. My husbands pickup was being invaded by mice! It was nasty. I tried mothballs trust me not plesant at all. The victor tri-kill was a much better solution. It kills three at a time and is easy to use. It also can be reused by removing the dead mice. I let my husband handle that. If you have a mouse problem give it a try.

This is a very creative mouse trap by Victor.  The Victor Tri-Kill Mouse trap does just that. Turn the trap upside down and bait it by placing a dab of peanut butter at the center of the trap.  Place trap along side a wall. When the mice stick their heads in the opening--well, that is the end of them. Once the mice are killed, they can be disposed of by emptying the trap and resetting it.Very well designed trap and easy to operate.  Once we caught 5 mice and one tail in the old-fashioned wooden traps.  This would have certainly been more efficient.  Cats work well too.

The Victor tri-kill mouse trap is an interesting pest control product. It is very easy to use and set. There is no chance of accidental injury. Baiting it was no problem. I was a little worried about how light it was.I baited the trap with peanut butter and set it. I placed in an area where we have tons of mice come in from the field. In that same area I have a bunch of traditional cheap sticky traps. I checked this trap for two weeks. I have often found it moved slightly from where I left it. But I have never found a mouse in it. The sticky traps in the same area are catching tons of mice. I can only conclude that this is not a great trap.There are some real pros to this design. Perhaps Victor can revisit it and make it a little more effective.

I had a mouse out in the garage that decided to take home there during the cold winter months.  I kept worrying that he was going to bring some of his friends or worse it was going to have babies and be a she.This product was an easy set up and cleanup after.  I have not seen anymore out there so I think I nipped this problem in the bud.Good product!

This trap is easy to set, you don't risk snapping your finger's off and they catch mice.  It is baited with peanut butter stuck to the "ceiling" and has the ability to catch up to three mice at a time.  We left it downstairs for several weeks and didn't catch anything, then stuck it behind the stove where we had actually seen a mouse, and caught two within twenty four hours.  We did not re-bait the trap so caught them with the same dried out peanut butter which was already there.I don't know how quickly it kills but they were dead when we found them.No batteries to run down, no electric parts to die on you. Reasonably priced enough that you can throw it away if the mouse gets too ripe before you check.Checking back in to update and buy more, for the basement, garage, and shop.

I had the chance to try this trap out and initially I thought it was a good design, but the more I played with it the more I learned I didn't like it. My issues are caused by this trap constantly triggering randomly for no reason. I also have a hard time resetting the traps, I have to push down several times to get it to lock back into place. I'm not sure if I have a defective one or not, but if I arm the trap within minutes I'll hear one of the traps spring and sometimes a second one follows. This is an interesting design, but the one I received just isn't working right.

It's a tiny mouse trap with one bait in the middle. The idea is to optimistically get 3 mice to buy the farm at the same time. I can see it take care of 1 mouse, but for it to catch three mice, 2 mice have to look at the first one and say "Well Fred's dead, but it won't happen to us". I have indeed caught one mouse in it. Not sure if the reason only one was caught was because only one was there. I'm optimistic too so I'm going to keep trying and will update my review if it catches more than one later on.

Victor is a reliable name in mouse traps and this did work, but so far just caught one (using peanut butter as bait), but it does allow up to three mice to be caught before either re-using or replacing. But, if cost is a concern this might not be the best choice.

Victor Tri-Kill Mouse Trap is a compact and reusable mouse trap that will help eliminate your pesky rodent problem.  The trap is easy to use and its ready out of the box.  All you have to do it bait the trap with peanut and spring it into action.  Those nosy and messy vermin wont know what hit them.  It's a lightweight and sturdy three trapper that will stand up to multiple uses.  Mice and voles will fall for it but if you have rats well that's a whole other issues.  But if mice and voles are creating havoc in your home then you'll need a Victor Tri-Kill Mouse Trap.  Up to three at a time, get 'em wholesale!
summary: Got a rodent problem?  This will help solve it for ya!

reviewText: I am not sure if I got them all with the wood traps, or if the mice just know better than to put their necks into a noose and signal the executioner; either way I have yet to catch any more in this trap.So, why do I like it? I have legitimate reasons. I have curious little dogs that I worry about getting their snouts snapped in the wood traps. I love the placement option for this trap. I love the easy setup of the chambers, and I love the convenience. With all of this love, but no mice yet, I still like it.If I witness any mouse activity while the Victor Tri-Kill is active, I assuredly will set the Victor wood traps again, bringing out the entire arsenal to determine which is more effective, and update accordingly. In the meantime, I feel very comfortable leaving the Tri-Kill set unattended, out of concern for the pets.

These mouse traps are ok. But they trip real easy and don't have all that much force to them. There's an excellent chance that if it catches any mice, they'll still be wiggling and squeaking when you find them. The trap is reusable, but that sounds like a tetanus shot waiting to happen. I'll give it a whirl, but last time we had a mouse, none of the newfangled stuff caught a thing, but the old style spring trap sure did. Sometimes tried and true is just the way to go. This one doesn't seem great.
summary: Meh, I'd Rather Use Standard Spring Traps

reviewText: This trap gets the job done, you can choose a bait basically kill three mouse with one stone. That it is reusable is also a plus...it's been very useful in our garage.

We have lived in this home since 1972 and had about 6 mice total over the years. We have woods close. A few years back had a few get in the basement. We used sticky traps and got them but they were still alive when found...all I can say is I was not the one to remove them and didn't ask details. Have not seen any for a few years but decided to sit this up just to make sure. So far no visitors. It is easy to set up and look at a glance to see if you have a catch. If we get any will come back and let you know. Personally I hope it works out like taking your umbrella and then it doesn't rain.I like this is pet safe as we also had so poison put out in the basement and keep the dog away. I placed this one so he cannot get to it in the garage as he loves peanut butter too.

Even though I have not caught a mouse in it yet I must say setting up and use is very simple. With small pets in the house we avoid using poisons and anything else our pets might happen upon and this  inexpensive and reusable trap is the answer to that.

This handy dandy little mouse trap is a 3-holer.  You can catch three mice at once. You can reuse it too, or for the faint of heart, you can just discard it when it has occupants.  This is perfect for us.  We have a rodent loving cat in the house, but she does not have access to the garage and that is where we have rodent visitors.  So we set traps in the garage. You can't help but love the fact that it can catch 3 at once and there is no poison involved, just good old fashioned mousetrap technology.

I thought we had some mices up in the attic so I got this and baited it for them, but nothing yet. Maybe we don't have mice? Once I'm positive we do I'll know if this thing works for sure. Until then, I'm neutral on it. One thing I wonder is, how dumb do they think mice are? If a mouse smells one of its kin or kind dying in this trap, or hears it squeal, how will two more mice be stupid enough to also climb in? Seems kind of silly, but who knows. One at a time seems more likely. We shall see. Mice seem purty smart from what I've seen. If there's no update to this, then it has neither failed nor succeeded. When it does either, I will add more here.

I really hate mice.  But, I also hated setting those blasted snap traps.  Can't count the number of times I nearly got snapped on, not to mention how often it went off just as I placed it down.  Also, the ick factor of a mashed head mouse was not a plus.  I had tried the adhesive traps, and they actually moved with some of the mice, also pretty gross.  Because we have a terrier, I was always worried he would get ahold of either the trap or decon, not to mentiona dead mouse that eated the poison.  I have to add that peanut butter is the best thing to use, no problem catching them then..However, since the dog also loves  peanut butter, it was a constant battle.  I use this in our outbuilding, and caught two mice straight away.  I check it regularly, and have seen no visible signs of additional rodents or droppings,and it's easy and safe to set.  Extra plus is that is reusable.  I also wear disposable gloves when I touch it, because I have been told that mice may avoid the smell of human hands.

Anyone who uses the classic wood-based spring traps to catch mice will know that they can be effective, but they can injure pets and careless fingers.  They don't always quickly kill the mice, leaving them to suffer long and excruciating deaths.  This trap reminds me of the old Victor 4-hole trap that my family used in the 1950's except this one is much easier to bait and set.  The old four-hole Victor trap had to be baited in four places and was much more difficult to set but it did the job.This trap has one central location for the bait and is much easier to set than any other mechanical trap that I've ever used.  It should be no hazard to fingers or to any non-rodent pets.  It's design guides the mouse into position for a certain, quick, choking death and it is easy to empty.  It's more expensive than the classic wooden-based spring traps, but I've found that it's just as effective and will, of course, catch more than one mouse if you have a serious infestation.
summary: Safer for Pets and Humans and More Humane

reviewText: First off, hands down Victor products are the best on the market. The #2 brand (Tom Cat) is awful - designed by the mice I think (LOL). Seriously, we vigorously tested about a dozen different methods in our warehouse, and the *only* brand that caught anything was Victor.That said, this trap does not perform as well as the traditional mouse trap. The traditional trap is easier for the mouse to find, easier to bait, snaps a little quicker & a little harder.HOWEVER ... this has enough perks, I still give it a strong recommendation for certain situations. It's a great option around kids, pets, or other animals (*not* safe around kids, but much more difficult to hurt yourself). It doesn't require nearly as much space (traditional traps will flip in the air when they snap, and unless they have a few inches of clearance, the mouse will get away). Also, the obvious advantage is that it's 3-in-1.For this trap, we're using it at home, hidden away between the kitchen cabinets and the wall. If a mouse ever wanders in, hopefully they'll find it... it's a "set it & forget it" insurance policy for us. Also great for a barn, shed, garage, basement, etc. I think the price is right (under $10), and it's reusable.
summary: Always go with Victor - the best in rodent control

reviewText: This may just be the easiest mouse trap I've ever set.  After removing the trap from the package (and removing the plastic insert beneath the trap), place peanut butter on the center piece labeled "BAIT."  Flip trap over and place the long straight edge along any wall experiencing mouse traffic.  If a mouse trips any of the traps, you can either discard the trap -- or discard the mouse and reset the trap.While the price tag might seem a bit much, it really isn't when I considered that this trap will catch three mice at once.

The Victor Tri-Kill Mouse Trap is a good idea in theory but in practice a trap to catch a single mouse is better.  This trap does not have separate sealed chambers but is more like a roofed room with three doors and no floor or interior walls.  It does not have a strong metal spring to instantly kill the mice but a bar that catches and strangles them while leaving them exposed.  I would prefer a single trap to catch & release the mice or if necessary, one that would kill them instantly and humanely over this method.

I hate mice, so when I found some droppings in the corner of my kitchen, I was really upset.  It was time to do something and to get rid of these guys once and for all.  I found the Victor Tri-Kill mouse trap and ordered it, it was the best thing that I ever did.  This will kill 3 mice at once and that is something that you definitely want to check out.

It's quite a bit of money for a mouse trap! But it does appear to be difficult to hurt yourself on this trap, that's a big plus, and it does have three separate entrances for catching three mice (baited with peanut butter). This is in our garage space just in case we have small rodent friends there. No kills yet. If you buy this trap, and clean and reuse it, it might not be a bad deal, but I suspect the theory is that people will catch 1-3 mice and toss the trap. In fact, there's a bit of a weirdness if you do plan to reuse it. If you catch a mouse, do you pick it up, clean up and reset it? Or leave the mouse? The former meant you only needed a regular mouse trap and the latter gets smelly. Maybe for a large mouse infestation, three per night?

You have to feel back for the lonely inventor, ever striving to make a better mousetrap. The design of this trap is creative, it's a snare (basically a plastic noose). However, in our tests in an old house, traditional snap traps continue to catch mice, and this one hasn't.

Traditional mouse traps have been around for a century. They work as well as anything, after all. Of course they get a bit nasty after one use (assuming you want to try and reuse one), they can be a bit tricky to set, and they'll catch pets or small children as easily as mice. This cleverly designed trap is simple to bait, simple to set (just depress the top), pet and child safe, can catch three mice on one setting, and it can be washed before reuse. It seems to catch mice just as well as the old fashioned type, too. If you've got more than one mouse to deal with, this trap is a good solution.

I had to wait a while to see if this worked. Finally, it caught a mouse. The plain old trap near it caught a mouse before this one did, but a lot has to do with placement, and circumstances. This trap is easy to set and easy to remove the mice. I have yet to see it in action catching more than one at a time, but it was nice to know that while one was caught in the trap, I still had two other sides ready to catch more.It's reusable, and the bait is hidden inside, so the mice can't steal the bait without springing the trap.

While this is a good looking trap, I can't say that it did much. I had it set up for a couple of weeks in my mother-in-laws house because she said she saw a mouse in her house. Well, I put three snap traps down, and the second night one snapped,and the following night another snapped. All were baited with peanut butter (the same brand). I can say that this is much safer than the snap traps, having almost snapped my fingers more than once. Other than that, there isn't much to say. I think it is an expensive product that does not do what it is supposed to do, at least for me. Out of all the traps I have used, the snap traps have been great.I also have an electric trap that is amazing, but it was VERY expensive becuase it will kill a large rat! So far, for me, nothing beats a snap trap....just watch your fingers. Of course, I do not have pets, and I don't put them where my kids can get at them. If this would have caught ANYTHING, I might have given it a better rating, but as it stands, I cannot. I will keep it baited (with fresh peanut better) and I will report back if things change, but I'm not holding my breath.
summary: Expensive and did not catch anything, but snap trap did!

reviewText: This trap is great b/c all you have to do is open the package and put it where you're having mice issues. For us it happened to be in our back yard shed. The trap works great and is easy to dispose of once your little pest finds his way in and dies. Overall, I'm very happy with this.

I do live in an area which probably attracts occasional mice, so I decided to try this.  Apparantly, my space hasn't been invaded yet, so I can only comment on the ease of baiting and setting it, and the fact that it's safe around pets.  So far, I'm happy with it for insurance purposes against pesky visitors.
summary: No mice yet, but am prepared

reviewText: I live on a river which, it turns out, practically guarantees me a new supply of rodentia as soon as I get rid of the current critters. Am I an expert on mousetraps? Well, noooo but I sure have tried everything short of poison and shotguns.This one is a good as any and better than many. I am relieved that my musician's fingers can't get hurt by the mechanism and that the little traps are easy to set. And that the mice are easy to remove after, well um, you know. There seems to be no suffering caused which is important to me since I have little option but to protect my food supplies and sanity but still would hate to see an injured rodent linger. I had a big ol' Tomcat trap that once caught Three Little Micies in one bang. But that was shear dumb luck. This one is designed for such devastation.

The main advantage to this awesome trap is the ease in setting and how safe it is for both your fingers and your pet's.  We were sorely needing a mouse trap in our barn but I was worried about having a "normal" snappy trap around our chickens... don't want to catch a bird instead of a mouse!  So this one REALLY worked great where we had other animals.  And you don't have to wince while setting it, waiting for it to snap on your fingers (or at least scare you).  The trapping aspect is really easy, you just put a tad bit of peanut butter inside in the spot labeled for it and you are pretty much set.  Set it in a place behind some furniture or another mouse runway (think darker, along the edge of the wall, more protected) and you will have excellent results.  It works great and protects my various livestock, so this is definitely a keeper!
summary: EASY to set, good for other animals being around, works!

reviewText: This is fine for larger mice.  It is easy to set: put peanut butter on the bottom of the trap, turn it over, close three doors.  When a mouse enters the trap it is supposed to walk over the trigger, which snaps.  We get tiny little mice that might be going under the trigger.  The basic Jawz mouse traps (strong plastic mouse traps) still seem to be the best option for our setting, with the addition of the sticky traps (which I hate) for catching the tiny ones that try to enter our home in the fall.  This is not the worst trap I have tried and like that it is easy to set, is easy to tell when it has sprung (the door pops up), and partially hides the mouse. However, I think I will stick with the Jawz or theD-Con 00027 Ultra Set Covered Snap Mouse Trap, although the D-Con can be very difficult to set.

Since a few weeks ago, I have changed my mind about this trap.  Now that it actually caught one mouse, I have to say it does work.  The mouse was a pretty small one and probably the smallest I have ever had get caught in a trap.  Small but I will take it.  It was very easy to remove the mouse from the trap (without toughing the mouse).  The trap reset very easy too, so it is waiting for the next one to enter.If I continue to have luck, I will revise this review to be more positive.
summary: very easy to bait and set

reviewText: I got this mouse trap for our hunting cabin, which has some mice on occasion.  The neat things about this trap are that the mechanism to set off the trap is internal and adjusts itself, without you having to twiddle with the triggers.  Also the mechanisms are internal, and therefore out dogs will not accidently set it off.  The location of the bait (they suggest peanut butter) is on the bottom inside the trap where the mice can smell it but can't really get to it.  Since each "trap" is really 3 different traps, capable of catching 3 mice at a setting, this thing is great and will catch a mouse along a wall no matter what direction he comes from.  I will set the trap out at the cabin this weekend and I feel sure if there is a mouse still in the cabin that this Tri Kill will get the little monsters.
summary: Cool idea for a mouse trap

reviewText: I have set thousands of mouse traps over the years, and am a firm believer that the "traditional model" has proved itself as a tried and true tool.  I have no problems looking into alternatives, however, and have had fun over the years catching mice of different species in everything from Sherman traps to a neat PETA- sponsored live trap (worked great).This trap, the Victor Tri-kill Moue Trap, is headed for the trash.  It's not that it can't catch a mouse.  It can.  After the first mouse, the trap is jerked around and moved away from its original placement.  Since mice are very neophobic, best success is for traps to be set right next to baseboards or known traveling lanes.  So I don't like that the trap moves from where I want it to be.  Second, the spring is just weak.  A traditional snap trap kills by causing extreme damage to a mouse, hopefully on the head and neck.  This trap seems to... strangle mice?  Aren't we past this level of revenge?  Finally, the trap is not robust in its construction.  One of the panels fell off as I was resetting it!A traditional snap trap is a much better, predictable, and reliable purchase.
summary: To be an improvement, it has to be better than the conventional snap trap...

reviewText: Any trap that will take care of three mice at one time is a good one. This would be perfect for a hunting cabin or shed; somewhere that you don't frequent very often. Three separate sections to kill three times without having to empty it all the time. It's reusable so you'll be able to kill again and again. Course, I wear gloves when touching reusable traps, this is no exception. Easy to use and at a price that won't break the bank, this might be one you want to try.

The idea behind this mouse trap is impressive--make three entryways for the mice so that even if they scurry past one side of it, they'll be suckered in by the smell wafting through the door on the other side. Well ... that didn't happen, despite having this set up in my garage for the past few weeks. I know there are mice in there because I can hear them. They must be laughing together over a few beers at the Hole in the Wall Bar at how ridiculous this baiter is.The trap itself is pretty much a no-brainer. You paste your peanut butter onto the plate, make sure all the doors are shut tight, and put it near a spot mice frequent (like right outside that Hole in the Wall Bar). If you think the bait has gotten a bit old, you can just wash it out under the faucet and paste some new stuff on.One plus on this trap is that the springs are all inside the trap, so it seems safe enough to leave around pets. Another plus is that there are no chemicals involved, and it definitely looks like it will kill quickly. Our mice seem to be smarter than the average critters, so perhaps we should just swap out the peanut butter for a smear of Guinness froth and catch some leprechauns instead.There is a 30 day warranty with this thing, and you're supposed to see the most mice caught on day 1, so even if this trap disappoints you as much as it did me, you can still get your money back.

This is easy to bait and easy to set up. I used peanut butter as the bait.  I put it in my garage where I have caught mice with single traps and killed mice with poison.  It has been there two weeks and so far no mice though the traps have sprung a couple of times without a mouse being killed.I am a bit uncertain about what to do if I catch a mouse.  Since this is reusable, I would have to press the lever down to release the mouse and remove its body by hand or with some sort of pliers or claw like device. I would rather throw out the whole trap than remove a mouse with my hands. If I do that this gets a lot pricier than the single use disposable traps.  Perhaps some sort of mouse remover mouse remover should be included with this if it is meant to be reusable.This is easier to use than many single use disposable traps. There is no danger of having the trap come down on a finger though I have used disable traps for years and never had that happen.I do think if this is meant to be reusable there should be an easier way of removing the dead mouse.

Mice don't stand a chance when it comes to the Victor Tri-Kill mouse trap. This trap is like three traps in one, with the bait in the center. Peanut butter actually works great with this trap, mice are attracted to it, and it sticks to the center of the trap. The trap is reusable, and is very easy to reset without worrying about getting fingers snapped. Because of the design, it easy to place against a wall and catch mice coming from any direction. The fact that it can catch up to three mice overnight is a huge bonus, and eliminates the need to worry about setting out multiple traps separately. The design is also much more visually appealing than the standard mouse trap design.

Let me start off by saying that I live in the country and have lots of mice problems. We also have kangaroo mice here, which seem to be just as smart as a regular mouse, but even more agile and acrobatic.Anyhow, we have traps set all the time-- I usually use the old-fashioned Victor trapsVictor Rat Trap  M201as they are pretty straight forward to set and cheap, and I can throw them away after use. We live in an area with bad hantavirus, so I'm not very interested in handling a trap a lot after it's been used. Still, we do take precautions with regular traps, so this trap just requires an extra couple of steps.The mouse came out of the trap just fine. I handled the trap with disposable gloves, after spraying it with a 10% bleach solution and letting it sit for 30 minutes. I then took the empty trap and put it in a 10% bleach solution to soak. If I had forgotten the mouse for a couple of days the cleaning would have been much more difficult and for me would not have been worth the risk of messing around with a gunky trap and I probably would have thrown it away.So, the bottom line? I will continue to use my old-fashioned Victors because they work well and I don't feel terrible about throwing away a little piece of wood with some bits of wire. This trap works well, but I wouldn't buy one because I know I would end up throwing it away after a few uses, and it is plastic. If I lived somewhere where there was no threat of hantavirus I would prefer to use this trap as it is so very very easy to set. I've set hundreds of the old style Victors, and there is still a startling snap! every once in a while. I think it would be quite difficult to hurt yourself with this trap, and you also don't have to worry about hiding the trap from pets (my 4 dogs are attracted by the peanut butter, so I always have to be very careful with hiding traps). So, I strongly recommend this to people in non-hantavirus areas.

Can you build a better mouse trap?  The answer is YES!  I had some mice in an outbuilding this Spring and purchased this new Victor TRI-Kill Mouse Trap to see how it would fair.  The trap is housed in a plastic covering and is, conveniently, I might add, already pre-set.  I baited my trap with crunchy peanut butter (just spread some on the underside of the trap) and place against a wall.The BIG question is... Did I catch three mice in one setting?  No, I didn't but I did catch TWO MICE in one night and honestly, if I would have had a third mouse in the building, I have no doubt that it would have caught three.This is a great product and can be reset VERY easily without worry of fingers getting in the way, children getting hurt or accidentally tripping the trap.  A TRULY GREAT MOUSE TRAP!
summary: Victor! The Only Name In Mouse Traps!  Great New Product!

reviewerName: Sir Charles Panther "Life is hard.  It's hard...
reviewText: How can you not just love a consumer product called "Tri-Kill?"  I mean, if there were a tri-kill recliner, I'd buy it.  If there were tri-kill 9000 tires for my car, I'd put them on.  If there were Post Tri-Kill Choco Poofs for my morning cereal, I'd be crunching away every morning.  Love that product title.The mice are in my house, no doubt about that.  I'm hearing them, even saw one a few weeks ago, the quick little bugger, and the glue traps in the attic are catching them.  But this product, now in place for approximately two months, has not caught a one.The product text is interesting in that it states mice are "very social animals, so...others congregate to the trap."  Really?  I'm no expert on Rodentia social behavior, but most animals that I have observed tend to scatter when one suffers a violent death.  Even the dumbest animals sense danger, and are smart enough to get away, and then stay away.  Doesn't the sight and stench of a dead mouse in the trap tend to serve as a bold warning to the others, much like the medieval gibbet, the rows of the crucified on the Appian Way, the ape skins on poles on the Planet of the Apes?  So how is it that a trap with a dead, rotting mouse in it is going to somehow attract another two?  This fundamental aspect of this trap doesn't make any sense to me.Positives of this product are that it's easy to bait and to set; this is intuitive, so you need minimal instruction and familiarity with the product (although there are ample and even illustrated instructions).  When set, even if it goes off there is no way it'll hurt you, as long as you're not so stoopit that you stick your finger in one of those little holes.  It holds no poison.  It's easy to tell when one of the three traps has sprung.The only negative I have is that it hasn't killed any mice.  In the time this has been in place and consistently re-baited in the garage, glue traps have managed to snag three mice.Bottom Line: it's billed as the latest high-tech improvement on a classic mouse-slaughtering design, but my recent experience with it--used exactly as directed--is that it's nothing more than a spring-loaded, peanut-butter-smelling garage floor ornament.

We have a mouse problem and found evidence of them in a large cupboard. So we cleared out the cupboard and set up this trap in there.I sort of wondered what the point was of having a trap that could theoretically trap up to three mice, since after it catches one, I don't plan on leaving it in the cupboard to wait until two more come along!It is not clear how quickly or humanely it will kill. It looks like it tries to suffocate the mouse, which is neither quick nor humane.We have cats, and hey have managed to catch and kill a few mice, but since they aren't keeping up with all the mice we supplement with traps. We have to be careful that the traps we use won't hurt the curious cats. This trap met those requirements. It won't hurt a paw stuck into it and likely won't get stuck on a paw either. No poison to worry about either.With the other single-mouse traps we have used, once one mouse is caught it seems like the remaining mice learn to avoid anything that looks or smells like the trap. I'm not sure if mice are really that smart, I'm just saying we didn't catch more mice until we switched up the kinds of traps we used.Setting the trap is not too difficult, though it took several tries to get it set. Be sure to look at the instructions long and hard as it can be easy to do it wrong. They recommend peanut butter as bait, which we have used in the past with success. There are no sharp parts in this trap at all.It appears the trap is made such that when tripped, a square plastic piece comes down edge-first and pinches the mouse at the neck. We have seen further mouse scat since putting in the trap but it hasn't tripped yet.The plastic piece that "squeezes" the mouse doesn't seem to have much force behind it, so I wonder how effective it is.I'll have to update this if it ever traps mice. Since I'm required to make a review of this product within 30 days per Amazon's new Vine guidelines, I don't feel I have had adequate time to see how it might work.

This is a rugged built mouse trap as opposed to those cheap little wooden snap traps.  I like that this trap will kill three mice rather than just one.The Tri-kill has three entrances and you should place it against the wall. They recommend that you bait it with peanut butter or any other bait that mice like. Each opening has a separate trap.  It can be reused until the spring wears out. I love that fact that it doesn't have poisons. Our other traps could harm our dogs so we have to keep the door close to that room in the basement.  A dead mouse in the trap will encourage others to come to the trap.  So far we have two dead mice in the trap.  Waiting for a third, then I haven't decided if I will clean it and reuse it or dispose of it.

I live in a rural area and have mice that get cold and so move in with me in the winter.  They don't ask; they just do it.  Not very friendly of them, so because of their attitude, I set out to kill them.  Poison works, but then I have mice dying in hidden places that then decay and make quite a smell for a time.  So my preferred method of mouse elimination is using traps.  The standard mousetrap is a brilliant piece of engineering and has stood the test of time.  However, this year I must have had smarter mice because they were able to eat anything I put on the traps without setting them off.I have no mice at this time because it is warm now and they must have moved back out or the poison did them in.  Either that, or they do not like my food and moved on to a better home.  So I really did not get a chance at murdering mice with this trap. But the trap does look capable, it is easy to set, and the design is such that I think the mice will not be able to steal the food without getting their little heads smashed.  But then, I thought that about the other traps also.  Anyway, just by examining this trap, I think it will work.  But until I squash a mouse, I will not know for sure.  I will know more this fall when the mice start moving in out of the cold.
This mouse trap is easy to set, bait, and includes suggested directions for placement.  After catching the mouse, the trap can be emptied and reset or can be disposed.

Pros: Nice build quality; easy to bait; very, very easy to set with no danger of nipping your fingers; nice, sensitive trigger snaps down hard after very light pressure applied.Cons: So far, the mice in my attic seem to prefer the old-school traps.  I've only had two since I set the Tri-Kill in place, but both avoided this in favour of my older traps.  I'm not sure that's truly a con, I think it's more luck of the draw.Since my trap is still unblooded I can't give a definitive answer, but I'm happy to keep this in place and I'm confident it will catch its share of any mice that pass its way.

In theory, these would be great. No finger mashing, easy clean up, no nastiness in the end. As an item it sounds perfect. We live in the country and field mice are terrible. They get into vehicles and into the mouse despite owning a lot of cats, so we know the mice are there. The problem thusfar has been that it has not produced results.I put these down three days ago, thinking it might be a viable alternative to the cruelty of older traps. Killing mice is not something I am fond of anyhow, and making them suffer seems horribly cruel. Sadly, they just seem to dismiss this and I have had to go back to baiting normal traps.I'll update if it catches a mouse and fill in more then, but it is still sitting there while the other traps are working.
summary: Good idea but has thusfar been ineffective.

reviewText: We generally don't have a large problem with mice in our area. In the past we've tried both the sticky strips and those cheap traps that you get four for a dollar some places. This trap looked pretty cool so I decided to give it a try.The design of the trap is excellent. You can really only use something sticky like peanut butter, but it sticks to the underside of the trap where the mouse can't actually really get to it. So realistically if the mouse ignores the fact that there are one or two other dead ones, the trap can keep working until all three are filled. The triangle design makes it very stable so it would be hard to tip over if a mouse was trying to fight it.There's a fair chance that it will be pretty messy you go to clean it out and if it's been a couple of days and things will have dried in there. At that point you're probably not going to want to risk any kind of contamination from the mice and just junk the trap. If you think you only have a few mice, then I would suggest this trap as clean, easier, and safer around kids or pets. However, if those aren't concerns then as long as you're willing to put up with those cheap ones occasionally failing (and sometimes catching your fingers painfully) they're probably the better choice if you think you have many mice. The only downside I have with this trap is that it can be expensive if you had to buy several of them.

I think I have tried every Victor trap they have ever made.  I have never had a mouse in my house until I bought this one that is nestled in the woods.  I have chickens and other pets that unfortunately attract mice.  Amazon offered these to me to review but I must tell you I was very happy with their snap trap that I purchased recentlyhttp://www.amazon.com/Kness-Snap-Rat-Trap-Pack/dp/B0007QKECG/ref=sr_1_39?ie=UTF8&qid;=1360342044&sr;=8-39&keywords;=victor+mouse+trap+packwhen I used this one I had had an infestation (to me) of about 15 mice and this trap killed them in less that a week.Since the I noticed some droppings on my counter and since this was up for my review I decided to try it.  This model is a covered trap which I prefer since I hate to see the dead little critters.  It is capable of getting three mice at a time.  I do not like killing anything but the mice I had in my house came down and were seen running around the living room floor my dog caught one in his mouth and the situation was getting dangerous.  Mice carry all kinds of disease.  It was either them or us..Now I took this trap and used peanut butter as they instructed and placed it by the wall as noted. It has been there for a week I no longer have any more mice.I love these traps they work well the only problem with this newer one is that you have to use peanut butter, I usually place cheese in the little well of the others but this does not have a well you must put peanut butter on it.  I cannot have peanuts so I had to buy a jar of PB and is is sitting in my closet beckoning me to eat it but I can't it is a waste for me to use the PB but that is the only problem I have with this product.
summary: Victor is the best traps around

reviewerName: Y. R. Wu "The will to win is nothing without ...
reviewText: After over a year, I haven't caught a single mouse, however in the same time I've caught about five mice with conventional snap-traps.  The bait wasn't even touched!  My hypothesis is that they can't smell the bait or are too timid to poke their head into the noose part of the trap.I even had the tri-kill out with NO snap traps for a good month, during that time there was clear evidence of mice, so I finally re-deployed the snap traps after which I caught two mice in quick succession.Sorry, but 2 stars until it catches somebody.Original review below...Here in Michigan the local field mice come into your garage every winter and eat up your grass seed and anything that's even slightly edible.The end of fall / start of winter is the peak where I can fill 2-3 mouse traps every other day.  I tried a "Nooski" trap recently but wasn't entirely impressed.  It was less prone to accidental release, but was moer tricky to set.This is almost foolproof - you press the three arrows down and it's set.  When it's tripped the arrow pops back up.One concern I have is that this has an internal bar which comes up to grab and kill the mouse.  My experience is that in cold weather the mouse can "Freeze" to the bar on a conventional trap making it hard to clear.  This strikes me as being worse since it's a fairly narrow loop.Since it's the end of winter, no mice caught yet. My neighbor has also been letting his cat roam so that's probably been a factor.  Will update later....
summary: After a whole year - not a single catch!

reviewText: I was sad to see my last Weber grill go....the tubes eventually rusted out, but not after at least 3 yrs. of all year round use!  I knew I wanted a Weber again.  Too many years before I had bought other brands only to have them die after one yr.  Researched this grill and read the reviews.
